newsitem.title: India: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - January 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - January 27.

text.p: Following is a summary of major Indian business and political stories in leading newspapers prepared for REUTERS by Business News and Information Services Pvt Ltd, New Delhi Tel:3324842, 3351006, 3761233 Fax:+91-11-3351006 Internet: biznis@giasbm01.vsnl.net.in
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch
for their accuracy.
TOP STORIES
The Times Of India
ASSETS OF FOUR LEADERS ATTACHED

The income tax authorities have provisionally attached assets of over 30 million rupees belonging to four Jharkhand Mukti Morcha party (JMM) leaders. The four were charged with accepting bribes to vote in favour of the Narasimha Rao government during the July 1993 no-confidence vote. The assets, including fixed deposits, savings accounts, residential flats, plots, vehicles and other expensive goods, belong to them and their family members. The income-tax department had also issued notice to the JMM leaders earlier this month pertaining to block assessment of their income for the previous few years.
Indian Express
SWEEPING CHANGES IN WAGE ACT LIKELY

The government, in an attempt to project a pro-poor and pro-worker image, proposes to amend wage laws covering the unorganised sector. The thrust of the proposed amendment is to ensure higher compensation to workers through wage revision every two years instead of the existing five. A part of the wage would be in cash thereby eliminating entire wage payment in kind as was being done in the agriculture sector. It also provides for more stringent penalties for violation of wage payment and work-hour norms by employers.
The Economic Times
PROVIDENT FUNDS TO BE REFORMED ON CHILEAN MODEL

The Finance Ministry has accepted the Chilean model to reform the functioning of pension and provident funds in India, with the larger objective of enhancing national savings. The Chilean model, cited as the most successful so far, allows workers to choose from several private pension funds. The companies, set up specifically to manage provident and pension funds, act within government guidelines and invest these funds profitably, giving workers the highest rate of return.
COMMITTEE TO STUDY COAL PRIVATISATION

The cabinet has referred an integrated coal policy to a committee of secretaries to further study deregulation of the pricing structure. The integrated policy, apart from deregulating prices, envisages the opening up of the entire coal mining sector to private investors. Major Australian coal mining companies have already initiated negotiations with state-run companies and domestic private sector players to set up joint ventures in this field. The opening up of this sector is expected to give a major boost and help dismantle the administered pricing structure of coal.
SAIL MAY PICK UP BRITISH COAL STAKE IN AUSTRALIAN MINE

The 16 billion rupee public sector major Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL) is negotiating with British Coal to buy out its 14.8 percent equity stake in the Golden Creek Mine of Australia. If this materialises, it would mark a significant step towards SAIL becoming a global company which will have easier access to quality coal from Australia. SAIL has already asked the British company for details related to the cost of investment in Golden Creek and the return SAIL may get from such an investment. The government favours SAIL investing in coal blocks abroad following a report which observes that a global coal shortage is expected to hike coal prices to unprecedented levels.
BROADCASTING LAW LIKELY TO FACE OPPOSITION

A proposed broadcast law, scheduled to come up before the cabinet for approval, is expected to face opposition from a number of leaders of the ruling coalition. The law proposes to cover all aspects of broadcasting in the country, including terrestrial broadcasting, direct-to-home broadcasting, local cable networks and private broadcast facilities. Objections to the proposed law seemed to have boiled down to the question of how much foreign equity should be allowed to companies in the sector. The proposal was to allow 49 percent foreign equity, which some ministers felt was far too high.
Financial Express
NO AUDIT EXEMPTION FOR GENERAL INSURANCE, SUBSIDIARIES

The General Insurance Corporation (GIC) and its subsidiaries are not exempted from auditing by the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG). Finance ministry sources said provisions in the Insurance Regulatory Authority (IRA) Bill notwithstanding, accounts of GIC and its four subsidiaries would continue to be audited by CAG. The Life Insurance Corporation had been exempted from CAG audit but similar relaxation was not likely to be extended to state-owned general insurance companies. Provisions regarding auditing of accounts by the IRA in the proposed bill did not seek to give any such relaxation to the GIC and its four subsidiaries from CAG audit.
MINISTRY URGES OPTIONS TO MEET OIL POOL DEFICIT

The Petroleum Ministry has asked the prime minister to consider options to meet the spiralling oil pool deficit, estimated to touch 147 billion rupees in March, 1997. The ministry was alarmed over the prospect of postponing a price hike in petro-products. The prime minister had met the finance and petroleum ministers to consider the fall-out in the oil industry following the ruling party's decision to defer a decision on the price hike. The options considered include a reduction in customs and excise duties on crude and petroleum products and the reimbursement of 44.29 billion rupees transferred from the oil pool account by the finance ministry to meet the fiscal deficit. The oil pool account is maintained by state-owned oil companies to manage a subsidy programme.
BIDS FOR 234 BLN RUPEE HIGHWAY PROJECTS SOON

The government will invite bids for 234 billion rupee worth of private investments in over 90 national highway projects to be developed in a few years. These bids are being offered for building railway overbridges, bridges, by-passes, expressways and widening of two-lane highways into four. Feasibility studies for most of these projects have been completed.
NATIONAL THERMAL POWER CORP SEEKS GUARANTEE

The state-run National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) has sought a 15-year guarantee for equipment supplied by Bharat Heavy Electricals (BHEL). NTPC insisted that each of its equipment be guaranteed for 100,000 hours. The guarantee was sought as a pledge from a bank which NTPC would be free to encash in the event of a breakdown of the equipment, NTPC sources said. NTPC was considering extending the guarantee condition to all other suppliers including Crompton Greaves and Kirloskars. But this would be done only after it was able to force BHEL to agree.
INFLATION RATE SLIPS TO 7.64 PERCENT

For the first time in 10 weeks, the annual rate of inflation fell marginally to 7.64 percent for the week ended January 11, 1997. Year-on-year inflation based on wholesale prices fell by 0.11 percentage points compared to 7.75 percent during the previous week. The wholesale price index for all commodities, however, remained unchanged at previous week's level of 319.8. Compared to this, annual inflation in the corresponding week in 1996 was 4.9 percent.
The Observer
CANADA CERTIFIES WHEAT IS TOXIN-FREE

The government, often accused of allowing the dumping of sub-standard goods in the domestic market, has extracted an assurance of quality from Canada on imported wheat. The import of 250,000 tonnes of wheat from Canada, contracted by the State Trading Corporation (STC), was under a cloud as the Canadian Wheat Board was reluctant to certify the grain as being free from toxic substances prohibited under Indian law. Inspite of requests from the commerce and food ministries request for a one-time relaxation of the requirements, the health ministry, forced STC to invite fresh tenders for import of wheat. Seeing the government's attitude, the Canadian Wheat Board agreed to issue the required certification.
FOREIGN FIRMS' ROLE IN DEFENCE OUTPUT SUGGESTED

Both government and private sector experts have recommended large-scale participation of foreign investors in defence production. The experts were of the view that open participation of multinational corporations (MNCs) would have no adverse impact on the country's security concerns. They suggested that there should be no inhibition on the part of the government in inviting them after a case-by-case scrutiny in areas such as the strategic electronics sector. With aims of increasing the defence infrastructure production base by more than five times by 2002 AD, the government proposes to create an increased capacity of nine billion rupees for both public and the private sectors in the sphere of strategic industry.
REPUBLIC DAY CELEBRATED WITH GUSTO

The country's military might and rich cultural heritage were on display at the 48th Republic Day parade in Delhi. Contingents from the armed and para-military forces took part in the annual parade with the president taking the salute. The Prime Minister of Trinidad and Tobago, Basdeo Panday, was the chief guest.
Business Line
MOVE TO CHECK WHEAT PRODUCT PRICES

Food Corporation of India (FCI), in an effort to put a lid on rising prices of wheat products, is trying for a measure of price control on them. The FCI has now allowed states the option to handle open sale of wheat to the millers, milling industry sources said. The scheme allows any state agency to allot wheat to millers and traders with a maximum ceiling of 500 tonnes per miller. But the price of wheat products would be fixed by the state government.
GENERAL INSURANCE CORP RESTRUCTURING TALKS BEGIN

The government initiated discussions for the splitting of the General Insurance Corporation (GIC) and its four wholly-owned subsidiaries into five distinct corporate entities. The restructuring would lead to a framework where GIC would be transformed into a company dealing exclusively with the re-insurance business. The four other companies would be involved in insurance policies.
